A '''paper key''' is a [[machine-readable medium|machine-readable]] print of a [[cryptographic]] key. The printed key can be used to decrypt data, e.g. archives or [[backup]] data. A  paper key can be the result of an [[offline private key protocol]]. The offline private key can also function as a token in [[two-factor authentication]].

The idea is that a digital key to decrypt and recover sensitive or personal data should have long-term durability and not be stored on any computer or network. The length of secure cryptographic keys restricts memorization, so the secret key takes the form of a 2D [[barcode]], a machine-readable print. Early implementations of a paper key by the company Safeberg use a [[Data Matrix]] [[barcode]]<ref>[https://www.safeberg.com/en/paperkey Safeberg Trusted paper key - 4.096 bits RSA key in a Datamatrix barcode] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715223101/https://www.safeberg.com/en/paperkey |date=2011-07-15 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lQJga--D0Do |title=Paper key: 4.096 bits RSA key in a Datamatrix 2D barcode |date=2010-03-02 |last=safeberg |access-date=2026-05-11 |via=YouTube}}</ref> or human-readable [[base 16]] digits.<ref>[https://www.jabberwocky.com/software/paperkey/ "Paperkey - an OpenPGP key archiver"] by [[David Shaw (technology writer)|David Shaw]]
</ref>

The user stores the printed key in a secure location. To avoid abuse, the key can only be used in combination with a ‘normal’ password.

The user can extract the key by creating a [[digital photo]] or scan of their paper key and feeding it to cryptographic software that extracts the key to decrypt the data.
